h1: The 7 Best Curved Ultrawide Monitors for Work and Play, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Curved Ultrawide Monitors: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 curved ultrawide monitors compared on panel type, curvature, refresh rate, USB-C, resolution and warranty at every price.
summary: The Alienware AW3425DW QD-OLED is the best curved ultrawide for people who want the best picture and a 240Hz refresh rate, and it costs more for it. The ASUS TUF FastIPS is the best mid-price upgrade for editing and gaming, the SANSUI is the value pick, and the Dell 34 Plus is the one to buy for a USB-C laptop desk.
intro: Curvature is the spec buyers misread most. A number like 1500R means the screen would form a circle with a 1500 millimeter radius, so a smaller number is a tighter curve. Tighter feels more immersive at a short viewing distance, but it also bends straight lines at the edges of a spreadsheet, and a gentler 1800R can be easier to live with. It is a comfort preference, not a quality grade.

This ranking weighs the things that do separate monitors. We reviewed seven 34 and 49 inch curved ultrawides from their spec sheets, comparing panel type, refresh rate, resolution, contrast, color coverage, connectivity and warranty, with price in buckets. No numbers come from our own measurements; every figure here is what the manufacturer or listing states.

products.name: Alienware AW3425DW QD-OLED
products.verdict: A 34 inch QD-OLED with a 240Hz refresh and the best contrast of any curved ultrawide here.
products.description:
The AW3425DW is a 34 inch QD-OLED curved at 1800R, with 3440 by 1440 resolution, 240Hz and a listed 0.03ms response time. It claims 99.3% DCI-P3 coverage, a 1,500,000:1 contrast ratio and HDR TrueBlack 400, plus G-Sync and FreeSync Premium Pro and a 3-year warranty. It sits in the $500 and up bracket.

It wins because QD-OLED switches each pixel off for true black, so a dark scene in a game or a film keeps its depth in a way no backlit panel can. The 1800R curve is gentler than the 1500R VA models, which suits people who dislike a tight bend. Against the Samsung Odyssey, you get a more manageable 34 inch width and a similar 240Hz refresh for much less desk space. The caveats are OLED traits: a text-heavy desktop shows slight fringing on some subpixel layouts, and static elements call for care over years of use.

Buy it if gaming, film and creative work share one screen, and your budget allows.
products.idealFor: Gamers and creators who want the best contrast and speed.
products.skipIf: You mainly work with static spreadsheets all day.

products.name: ASUS TUF FastIPS
products.verdict: A 34 inch FastIPS panel with 250Hz, the quickest refresh short of OLED.
products.description:
The ASUS TUF FastIPS is a 34 inch curved panel at 1500R with 3440 by 1440 resolution, 250Hz and a listed 0.5ms response. Static contrast is listed at 4000:1, well above what typical IPS panels manage, and it covers 95% DCI-P3 with a 3-year warranty. It falls in the $200 to $500 bracket.

Its second place is earned by combining a fast refresh with the color stability of an IPS-type panel. Unlike VA screens, IPS-type panels keep colors and brightness consistent as you move off-center, which matters for photo and video work on a screen this wide. Against the SANSUI VA, you pay more for 250Hz and better angles; against the OLED, you give up contrast depth but also OLED's static-image caution.

Choose it for editing and gaming on one monitor. The listing mentions no USB-C, so connect a laptop through DisplayPort or HDMI.
pros: Fastest refresh outside the OLED pair
products.idealFor: Photo and video editors who also game.

products.name: SANSUI 34" Curved Ultrawide
products.verdict: A 200Hz VA ultrawide with HDR and picture-by-picture, aimed at first-time buyers.
products.description:
The SANSUI is a 34 inch VA panel curved at 1500R, at 3440 by 1440 and 200Hz with a 1ms response. It lists 97% DCI-P3, 130% sRGB, 3000:1 contrast, HDR, and PiP/PBP modes. It is in the $200 to $500 bracket.

It takes third place because it packs the most features per dollar. The 3000:1 contrast of VA gives deeper blacks than IPS panels at this price, and PiP/PBP lets you split the screen between two inputs, which is handy for work and entertainment. Against the ASUS above, you give up 50Hz and IPS viewing angles. Against the Alienware VA, the listing is less clear about warranty and stand adjustment.

Buy it as a first curved ultrawide. Be aware that the listing does not state warranty length.
products.idealFor: First-time ultrawide buyers watching their budget.

products.name: Alienware AW3425DWM
products.verdict: A 180Hz VA ultrawide with HDR400, a console mode and a height-adjustable stand.
products.description:
The AW3425DWM is a 34 inch VA curved at 1500R, with 3440 by 1440 resolution, 180Hz and a 1ms GtG response. It lists 3000:1 contrast, 95% DCI-P3, HDR400, a dedicated console mode, height adjustment and a 3-year warranty. It sits in the $200 to $500 bracket.

Fourth place suits it because its strengths are practical rather than headline-grabbing. A height-adjustable stand is a basic ergonomic feature that some ultrawides skip, and a console mode tunes the screen for an Xbox or PlayStation. Against the SANSUI, you give up 20Hz of refresh and gain a warranty and stand. Against the Dell, you give up USB-C charging.

It is a sound choice for a gamer who also uses a console. The caveat is the same VA trade as the others, with narrower viewing angles than IPS.
products.idealFor: PC and console gamers sharing one screen.
products.skipIf: You want to charge a laptop over USB-C.

products.name: Dell 34 Plus USB-C (S3425DW)
products.verdict: A 120Hz VA ultrawide with 65W USB-C charging and Dell's panel warranty.
products.description:
The Dell S3425DW is a 34 inch VA at 1500R and 3440 by 1440, running at 120Hz with a listed 0.03ms response. It claims 3000:1 contrast, 99% sRGB and 95% DCI-P3, USB-C with 65W power delivery, and Dell's Premium Panel warranty. It sits in the $200 to $500 bracket.

It ranks fifth because its focus is the office rather than the esports. USB-C with 65W delivery lets one cable carry video, data and charging to a laptop, which cleans a desk and covers most thin-and-light laptops. The 120Hz refresh is fine for work and casual games but trails the 180 to 250Hz models above. The sRGB coverage figure is a useful number for office and web work.

Buy it for a hybrid work desk. Skip it if competitive gaming matters most.
products.idealFor: Remote workers who plug in a laptop every day.

products.name: ASUS TUF VG34VQ3B
products.verdict: A 180Hz VA ultrawide with four USB 3.2 ports, speakers and a 3-year warranty.
products.description:
The VG34VQ3B is a 34 inch VA curved at 1500R and 3440 by 1440, with 180Hz and a 1ms MPRT response. It lists 90% DCI-P3, four USB 3.2 ports, built-in speakers and a 3-year warranty, in the $200 to $500 bracket.

Sixth place follows from color: 90% DCI-P3 is the lowest coverage figure in the group, and for creative work the others do better. Where it shines is connectivity. Four USB 3.2 ports serve a keyboard, mouse and drives without a separate hub, which is the most in this ranking. Note that MPRT is a motion-blur measure with backlight strobing, not the same as a gray-to-gray response, so compare it carefully.

Pick it for a gaming desk with many peripherals. Creative users should look at the ASUS FastIPS.
cons: MPRT is not a GtG figure

products.name: Samsung Odyssey G93SC 49"
products.verdict: A 49 inch QD-OLED at 5120 by 1440, with the most screen of any monitor here.
products.description:
The Odyssey G93SC is a 49 inch QD-OLED curved at 1800R, at 5120 by 1440 and 240Hz with 0.03ms response. Contrast is quoted at 1,000,000:1 and color coverage at 99% DCI-P3, with both G-Sync and FreeSync Premium Pro supported alongside PbP. It is in the $500 and up bracket.

Seventh place is a matter of fit, not quality. It is the same pixel height as the 34 inch models but twice the width, equal to two 27 inch screens side by side, which is wonderful for racing sims, trading boards and timelines but demands a deep desk and a strong stand or arm. Against the Alienware OLED, you pay for width rather than a sharper image.

Buy it if you want a monitor wall in one panel. Measure your desk first.
cons: Needs a very deep, wide desk
products.idealFor: Simmers and traders who want maximum width.
products.skipIf: Your desk is under about 30 inches deep.

whatMatters.detail: VA panels deliver deep blacks and strong contrast at a good price but have narrower viewing angles. IPS-type panels keep color consistent across the width of the screen. QD-OLED gives per-pixel black and the best contrast, with caution about static images. Pick the panel before you pick the brand.

1500R is a tight curve, and 1800R is gentler. A tighter curve suits a shorter viewing distance and gaming immersion. A gentler curve distorts straight lines less in spreadsheets and design tools. Sit about an arm's length away and judge which you prefer.

A 3440 by 1440 panel at 180Hz or more is smooth for competitive games, while 120Hz is fine for work. Check which response metric is quoted, since gray-to-gray and MPRT are different. Your graphics card must also drive the resolution at that frame rate.

USB-C with power delivery, here 65W on the Dell, lets one cable charge a laptop and carry video. A USB hub adds convenience for peripherals. Confirm the video inputs too, and check that HDMI supports the full refresh rate at 3440 by 1440.

A 3-year warranty is common on better models, and OLED panels in particular benefit from clear burn-in coverage. A height-adjustable stand matters for posture, and if the stand is limited, plan to use a VESA arm.

howToChoose.intro: The panel decides how the monitor looks every day.

cards.label: 34 inch ultrawide
cards.text: 3440 by 1440 fits most desks, works well with standard stands and costs less. It is the safe choice. Picks: Alienware AW3425DW, ASUS TUF FastIPS, Dell, SANSUI.

cards.label: 49 inch super-ultrawide
cards.text: 5120 by 1440 replaces two monitors but needs a deep desk and a sturdy mount. Pick: Samsung Odyssey G93SC.

howToChoose.note: Default to 34 inch unless you truly want a monitor wall.

howToChoose.subheading: For Photo and Video Editing Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: High DCI-P3 coverage, stable viewing angles and a clear panel type. IPS-type or QD-OLED beats VA for consistent color across the screen.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: ASUS TUF FastIPS for stability, Alienware AW3425DW for contrast, and the Dell for sRGB web work.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You game and watch films on the same screen, or you want the best contrast available. The Alienware AW3425DW QD-OLED is the upgrade.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The monitor is for office work and casual games. The SANSUI or Dell covers that under $500.

faq.q: Will my graphics card drive 3440 by 1440 at high refresh?
faq.a: It depends on the game. Many mid-range cards handle 3440 by 1440 at 100 to 144 fps, and a 240Hz screen benefits mostly in esports titles or with a strong card.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake buyers make?
faq.a: Buying on refresh rate alone. A 250Hz screen with a poor panel is worse for movies and editing than a 180Hz screen with better contrast or color.

faq.q: Is OLED worth it over VA or IPS?
faq.a: For contrast and motion, yes, and the Alienware QD-OLED is the clearest example. For long static spreadsheets and high ambient light, a VA or IPS-type panel is a safer pick.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Use the highest refresh rate from the DisplayPort cable, enable adaptive sync in the monitor menu and graphics driver, and set Windows scaling to a comfortable level. Adjust the stand so your eyes meet the top third.

faq.q: Do I need to worry about burn-in?
faq.a: On OLED, yes in principle. Use dark mode, hide taskbars, and let the panel's refresh routines run. Check the warranty wording, as the Alienware lists 3 years.

faq.q: Can a curved ultrawide mount on a VESA arm?
faq.a: Most can, but check the weight and VESA pattern first. A 49 inch panel needs a heavy-duty arm, and a 34 inch model usually works with a standard gas-spring arm.

finalTake: The Alienware AW3425DW QD-OLED is the best curved ultrawide for anyone who values contrast and speed, and the ASUS TUF FastIPS is the better balance for editing and gaming at a mid price. The SANSUI is the sensible value, the Dell is the USB-C desk monitor, and the Samsung is for those who want a monitor wall. Decide on panel type and desk depth first.
